name: Ridge Traverse Route
prior_findings: Summit-day gain 1,600 ft is impossible from the ~6,050 ft camp to the 7,869 ft summit; no source stated day or total gain in pass 1. Never compute a figure; only set one two sources state.

earlier_research.correct_value: Crescent Creek Basin camp (a little over 6,000 ft, below Mount Terror), reached over the Barrier
earlier_research.evidence: The Rake sits on the crest between Mount Terror and the Twin Needles and its only route starts from the Terror-Rake notch, which rises from Crescent Creek Basin; one source lists the Rake among the peaks bordering Crescent Creek, another places the standard Crescent camp below Mount Terror at 6,050 ft with the Rake beside Terror, and a third shows Terror Basin (5,800 ft) faces the Barrier, Degenhardt, Pyramid, Inspiration and the McMillan Spires instead. The row's own waypoints, approach variant, descent and bail already put the climb on the Crescent Creek side; only the itinerary named Terror Basin.

earlier_research.correct_value: About 2,000 ft up and down on summit day (camp a little over 6,000 ft to the 7,869 ft summit); car-to-car itinerary total 8,100 ft
earlier_research.evidence: Camp in Crescent Creek Basin is at about 6,050 ft and the summit is 7,869 ft, so the summit day needs at least ~1,820 ft of climbing plus the ups and downs of the rubble gully; the 1,600 ft figure was impossible from either the old 5,800 ft or the corrected camp. The row's high point, summit schedule and day note all say 7,869 ft. gain_ft is raised to match the new itinerary total (5,800 + 2,000 + 300); loss_ft is left untouched per the loss rule.

earlier_research.correct_value: Terror Basin and Crescent Creek cross-country zones are walk-up only (in person at Marblemount); only Boston Basin, Eldorado, Sulphide, Price, Triumph and Tapto Lakes can be reserved in advance
earlier_research.evidence: The park's cross-country zone page and its backcountry reservations page both state that only Boston Basin, Eldorado, Sulphide, Price, Triumph and Tapto Lakes can be reserved in advance and that all other cross-country zones are walk-up only; Terror Basin and Crescent Creek are in the zone table but not on the reservable list. A trip report confirms the Crescent Creek permit was picked up in person at Marblemount. The camp cards already said walk-up only; the itinerary, access card and permit text are corrected.
The route's first-ascent account grades the Rake IV 5.9, and the row's grade, rock_grade, pitch_detail and itinerary all say 5.9; the 5.7 partner skill is the only outlier.

The only published account says just that the party rappelled from the Rake's summit (they were continuing west along the traverse), with no count or station detail. No source supports the three numbered rappels in rappel_detail, which the row itself admits are estimated from pitch count; the rappels prose ('number unknown') is the accurate one. Recommend removing or relabelling the three-row table by hand; no patch written.

The summit waypoint says 7,840 ft (elev and elevFt) while high_point_ft, the overview and itinerary say 7,869 ft. One topo-derived list gives 7,869 ft; another listing reports 7,840 ft (likely the map contour). Could not reach a second topo source to confirm, so no patch.

Retry searched further Rake/Southern Picket trip reports. The enchainment account and later reports mention only rappelling from the Rake's summit (and separate raps into the Terror col off Mount Terror), never a number of rappels or stations for the Rake itself. The rappels prose ('number unknown') remains the supportable statement; the three-row table is an estimate with no outside support. Settled only by a party that descended the Rake and recorded its stations.

One topo-derived list gives 7,869 ft; the peak-list/Wikipedia-style listing gives 7,840 ft. A USGS 3DEP point-elevation grid of 49 samples around the summit pin peaks at ~7,825 ft (pin itself 7,822 ft), which is below both and cannot adjudicate a sharp spire where the DEM undershoots. Sources genuinely disagree; settled by a surveyed or LiDAR spot height for the summit.

earlier_research.correct_value: $10 per person (not per night) plus a $6 nonrefundable fee, charged mid-May to early October.
earlier_research.evidence: The NPS fee-structure release states '$10 per person plus a $6 nonrefundable permit fee' with no per-night basis, charged mid-May through early October; the Spokesman-Review report on the March 2024 change gives the same per-person structure for the whole permit. The NPS reservations page lists the recreation fee as '$10 per person'. One park-fund explainer says per night, but the park's own pages and the news coverage agree on per person. access.permit is aligned with access.fees.

approach_logistics.peakLat/Lng (48.768, -121.288) is not the Rake's summit and matches the coordinate other Southern Pickets rows use, while the summit waypoint (48.7755, -121.3067) agrees with the area coordinate. Coordinates are out of scope for this pass (no patch allowed); a coordinate pass should set peakLat/Lng from the summit waypoint after checking a topo-derived coordinate for The Rake.

The summit waypoint says 7,840 ft while itinerary day 2 says 7,869 ft (in the note and the schedule). One topo list gives 7,869 ft and a Pickets trip-report index gives 7,840 ft, so the two outside records disagree just as the row does; a USGS/interpolated topo figure would settle which to adopt.

earlier_research.evidence: itinerary.totalNote says ~8,100 ft of gain round trip, but gain_ft is 7,700 and the itinerary days sum to 7,700 (5,800 + 1,600 + 300). No outside source stating the car-to-car gain for this route was found, so neither figure can be confirmed; a source for the total would settle it.

row.name: Ridge Traverse Route
row.fa: Wayne Wallace, Colin Haley, Mark Bunker — July 26, 2003 (first ascent, climbed during their four-day Complete Southern Pickets Traverse)
row.description: The east ridge of The Rake (IV 5.9) — the only known technical route to the summit — was first climbed July 26, 2003 by Mark Bunker, Colin Haley, and Wayne Wallace during their 'Walking the Fence' complete Southern Pickets enchainment. It is almost always climbed as one leg of a larger Southern Pickets traverse rather than as a stand-alone objective.
gear: Alpine rock rack to ~3 inches (mixed nuts and cams) for the ridge climbing
A few pitons and a light hammer — the route bypasses a loose gully via a short section of vertical-to-overhanging rock that the first-ascent party protected on pitons rather than clean gear
60m rope, doubled for the rappel off the summit
Cordage/slings for a rappel anchor at the summit
hazards: Loose, rubble-filled gully directly below the route's initial vertical/overhanging rock — the main rockfall hazard
Sustained, exposed climbing along a narrow, serrated ridge crest with limited retreat options
Remote, glaciated approach terrain in the Terror/Crescent Creek basins — crevasse and steep snow hazard, especially early season
Fast-changing North Cascades weather; rain or snow can move in within hours even in mid-summer
row.overview: The Rake is a serrated, ~7,869 ft summit in the Southern Pickets, on the ridge crest between Mount Terror and the McMillan/Himmelhorn group above upper Crescent Creek Basin. Its jagged, saw-toothed skyline — visible from the Terror Basin/Crescent Creek approach — gives the peak its name. The only documented technical route, the east ridge (IV 5.9), was first climbed July 26, 2003 by Mark Bunker, Colin Haley, and Wayne Wallace during their 'Walking the Fence' complete Southern Pickets enchainment. Nearly all recorded ascents of The Rake come as one leg of a larger Pickets traverse rather than as a stand-alone objective.
row.beta: The East Ridge route involves vertical to overhanging rock on pitons to avoid a loose gully below, followed by approximately half a mile of alpine ridge climbing. The route was established as a first ascent during the Complete Southern Pickets Traverse in July 2003. Access is gained via a snow and scree approach from the Mount Terror/Rake notch.
row.turnaround: Ensure you reach the base of rock climbing by mid-morning to allow time for the technical sections and descent before afternoon weather deteriorates. Turn back if conditions are unsafe or if you lack the climbing grade to safely manage the vertical sections.
row.rappels: Rappel from the summit (number of rappels unknown)
row.permit: North Cascades NP complex: no permit for day climbs; all overnight backcountry stays require a backcountry permit (this cross-country zone is walk-up only, issued in person at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center).
row.comms: No cell service in the Picket Range. Satellite communicator or emergency beacon recommended for this remote alpine terrain.
obj_haz: Loose rock / rockfall in the approach gully below the route
Extreme remoteness — multi-day commitment with no quick bailout
Rapid weather changes typical of the Pickets crest

row.detailed_rack: Alpine climbing rack suitable for Grade IV rock: selection of carabiners and quickdraws, 60m multi-pitch rope setup, pitons for protection on vertical sections and loose terrain, helmet for rockfall hazard in gully approach
pro_tips: Combine with adjacent Southern Picket towers
row.pro_needs: Grade IV rock climbing ability required. Protection essential on vertical to overhanging sections. Firm grounding in alpine rock climbing, loose terrain assessment, and objective hazard evaluation necessary.
row.best_season: Mid-July through early September is most reliable, once snow has receded from the approach gullies and basins. Earlier-season attempts should expect firm/steep snow on the Terror or Crescent Creek approach and possible verglas on the ridge.
row.approach: From the Goodell Creek Trailhead off the North Cascades Highway (SR-20) near Newhalem, follow the Goodell Creek climbers' path, crossing two branches of the creek before a steep, cairned ascent (roughly 4 miles in) into the Terror Creek drainage. From there, either climb the steep Terror Basin route (about 2.5 miles, ~4,700 ft gain, faint tread, dense brush, and a class 3 root-pull section at a cliff band) or take the more direct but notoriously brushy Crescent Creek Basin line to reach a high camp below The Rake's east ridge. Expect a long, unmarked, bushwhack-heavy day-plus approach typical of the Pickets — there is no maintained trail.
row.descent_text: There is no walk-off descent. Parties rappel the east ridge back toward the Crescent Creek side, or, when climbing The Rake mid-traverse, continue over talus and snow below the Twin Spires to a camp on the west side before proceeding toward Himmelhorn.
row.bail: Reverse the approach over the Barrier.

fitnessSpec.hiking: Very high — the Crescent Creek approach into the Southern Pickets involves sustained off-trail bushwhacking, steep brush/talus, and significant elevation gain typical of Pickets approaches; expect a full, grueling approach day(s) before any climbing begins

partner_requirements.approachTime: Multi-day approach typical (1-2 days in via Crescent Creek basin) given the remoteness and difficulty of the approach; not a single-push objective for most parties

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: Mid-July through early September, with conditions generally most reliable in a narrower core window of late July through August once approach snow has melted out

July.reason: Early July can still hold lingering snow on approach slopes and the basin; conditions firm up through the month, matching the start of the best-season window

August.reason: Most reliable month — driest rock, most consistent approach conditions, and the core of the documented Jul-Sep season

September.reason: Early September can still be good, but the season ends early in the month; later-season storms and shortening daylight increase risk for a route this remote

weather.typical: For a North Cascades National Park alpine objective: rapid weather changes are common, and the remoteness magnifies the consequences of any storm moving in
weather.probability: Afternoon thunderstorms and fast-moving fronts are a known North Cascades summer pattern

seasonal_hazards.exposure: High — sustained exposure along a serrated alpine ridge with loose rock throughout, in a setting where a fall or injury is far from help given the remoteness

approach_variants.name: Crescent Creek Basin to the Terror col
approach_variants.notes: From the Goodell Creek trailhead follow the climbers' path up the old roadbed, crossing two branches of the creek, then take the steep cairned ascent into the Terror Creek drainage. Either climb the Terror Basin line — faint tread, dense brush and a class 3 root-pull section at a cliff band — or the more direct but notoriously brushy Crescent Creek Basin line, to a high camp beneath the peak. There is no maintained trail anywhere on this approach and it is a long day or more of unmarked bushwhacking.
approach_variants.season: Mid-July to September, once the basins are melted out enough to camp and travel
hazards: Rubble-choked entry gully with continuous rockfall potential
Very steep rock immediately off the notch, with old fixed pins rather than modern anchors
About half a mile of serrated alpine ridge above, with committing terrain and no easy escape
approach_variants.baseFinding: The base is the low notch between Mount Terror and this peak, and the way in is a single deep, rubble-choked gully running up to it. Climb that gully staying RIGHT, on slightly harder but far more solid class 3 rock, rather than wading up the debris in its bed. From the notch the ridge starts immediately above on very steep, vertical to overhanging rock, taken directly precisely in order to avoid the loose gully below and to the side of it; the first ascent drove pitons here, so old fixed pins are what you may find rather than bolts. The proof is that the hard climbing begins at once, off the notch, with no walking terrain in between — if you are standing on easy ground hunting for a start, you are in the wrong place. Beyond it the climb becomes roughly half a mile of serrated ridge, which is where the peak's name comes from. Check your orientation in the notch: Terror's bulk should be on your EAST and the saw-toothed crest you are climbing on your west.

bivy.name: Crescent Creek Basin camp
bivy.notes: Crescent Creek Basin sits on the north side of the crest and is what you cross the Barrier for, reached over the roughly 6,400 ft saddle northeast of the Chopping Block. It is the working base for East and West McMillan Spire, Inspiration, the Twin Needles, and for the Ottohorn and Himmelhorn by way of the col between them; Frenzel Spitz sits off the main chain near the Ottohorn's north side. Parties camp at several benches at different heights.
bivy.water: Snowmelt streams and pools fed by the basin's snowfields, reliable early and mid season and unreliable late once the snow has pulled back. Plan on melting snow in a lean year.
bivy.permit: This is the SEPARATE Crescent Creek cross-country zone, not Terror Basin — a trip camping in both needs both zones written onto the same permit, night by night. Like Terror Basin it is walk-up only at Marblemount rather than bookable in advance.
bivy.capacity: A few parties on gravel, slab and snow; the zone is capped at 6 people per party

bivy.name: Goodell Creek Campground, roadhead staging
bivy.notes: The pavement-level staging camp rather than a mountain camp, and most parties use it to get a few hours of sleep before starting the approach in the dark. Bear boxes, tables and vault toilets mean food and rubbish can be dealt with before you leave the car. Sleeping here advances you toward the peaks not at all, but it does let you hit the roadbed at first light, which matters on an approach this long.
bivy.water: Potable water when the campground is open for the season; the Skagit and Goodell Creek are immediately adjacent as backup
bivy.permit: Frontcountry campground fee only — no wilderness permit needed to sleep here. Reservable through recreation.gov in peak season, first-come outside it; not always open year round, so confirm before counting on it.
bivy.capacity: 19 individual drive-in sites, plus a separate group campground where the old roadbed begins

bivy.name: Old Goodell Creek roadbed near the Terror Creek crossing
bivy.notes: The roughly four miles of overgrown roadbed to the cairn near the Terror Creek crossing is walking rather than climbing, and a party leaving the car late often ends the first day somewhere near here. That is defensible, because the ground above is where the day gets expensive and nobody wants to be finding the path by headlamp. The cost is that the whole climb to the basin still lies ahead, so a low night usually means a full second day of approach with no climbing in it.
bivy.water: Reliable year round from Goodell and Terror Creeks; the last certain running water until the climbers' path regains streams high in the timber
bivy.permit: A wilderness permit is required, and this spot is LEGALLY AWKWARD: cross-country camping in the park is meant to be at least half a mile from a trail and a mile from designated camps, and the old roadbed is a trail. Ask the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center where they will place you before you plan on it.
bivy.capacity: One or two small parties on flat ground beside the old grade

bivy.name: Terror Basin camp
bivy.notes: The standard base for the south side of the range, and the place the Terror Creek climbers' path is trying to reach. From the flat gravel the basin runs up to a notch on its eastern rim near 6,200 ft, and the Chopping Block, Degenhardt, the Pyramid and the west side of Terror are all workable from here. Whether a party gets this far on day one is genuinely contested — strong parties who know the path do it, and parties who lose the path in the timber routinely do not.
bivy.water: Meltwater off the snowfields above the basin, generally dependable while snow remains and a hunt in a dry late summer. Sources are seasonal, not spring-fed.
bivy.permit: Terror Basin cross-country zone, from Marblemount. 6-person party maximum. It is NOT on the short list of zones reservable in advance, so it is WALK-UP ONLY — up to 24 hours ahead, with permits released in the morning of day one. Fires prohibited; human waste in a cathole, or out in a blue bag above treeline.
bivy.capacity: Small flat gravelly ground for a few tents; the park caps the zone at 6 people per party

bivy.name: Stump Hollow bench
bivy.notes: Stump Hollow is the open slabby heather ground at timberline between the Barrier ridge and the Chopping Block, and the first place after the forest where a tent actually goes down comfortably. Parties heading for the north side use it as the intermediate camp, because an easy rising traverse reaches the saddle northeast of the Chopping Block near 6,400 ft and drops into Crescent Creek Basin from there. Camp on rock, gravel or snow rather than the heather — this is thin alpine ground that shows every night somebody spends on it.
bivy.water: Snowmelt only. Trickles and small pools are dependable through early summer while snow lingers, and can dry up or retreat entirely by late season; late-summer parties should expect to search or carry.
bivy.permit: Cross-country zone permit from the Wilderness Information Center. This bench sits close to the divide between the Terror Basin and Crescent Creek zones, so ask which zone the rangers are writing you into rather than assuming — the answer decides what the rest of your itinerary can say.
bivy.capacity: Small — a couple of parties on heather benches and slabs, and it is easy to end up spread out

bivy.name: High bivouacs at the western end of the crest
bivy.notes: The western summits — the Twin Needles, Ottohorn, Himmelhorn and Frenzel Spitz — are far enough along the crest that a party working from a basin camp faces a very long day, so some take a bivouac high on the traverse instead. These are improvised spots rather than established sites, and quality varies from a decent gravel bench to a night sitting on a ledge. There is no shelter and no water, so this only makes sense with a settled forecast and a party willing to move fast the next morning.
bivy.water: No dependable source. These are snow-and-rock bivouacs: carry water up or melt snow, and expect nothing at all once the summer snow has gone.
bivy.permit: Still inside a cross-country zone and still requires a wilderness permit with the night assigned to the correct zone. Camp only on snow, rock or bare ground, keep 100 ft from water, no fires, and carry waste out in a blue bag above treeline.

name: Standard Scramble (First Divide / Marmot Lake approach)

row.overview: Mount Hopper (6,120 ft) is a deep-interior Olympic summit in the Daniel J. Evans Wilderness of Olympic National Park, on the Skokomish–Duckabush divide near First Divide. Its line parent is Mount Steel (6,612 ft), about 1.96 miles west-northwest; Mount Duckabush, Mount LaCrosse, and White Mountain are also nearby. The peak is named for brothers Stanley and Roland Hopper, sons of a Singer Sewing Machine Company executive — Stanley took part in W. G. Steel's 1906 ascent of neighboring Mount Steel. The standard Class 2 line is straightforward climbing, but the historically standard Staircase/North Fork Skokomish approach has been closed since the 2025 Bear Gulch Fire, and so has the Home Sweet Home Trail over First Divide that the longer Duckabush River Trail alternative needs, with no reopening date on the park's trail-conditions page updated September 14, 2026.
row.beta: This is not a technical climb but a serious backcountry scramble: about 13.1 trail miles from the Staircase trailhead to First Divide/Home Sweet Home camp, then off-trail travel east over talus, heather benches, and a short rocky ridge to the summit. Most parties backpack in and camp at Home Sweet Home (just below First Divide) to split the approach over two days. A shorter but steeper off-trail alternative climbs from Lake of the Angels (reached via the Putvin Trail), crossing the ridge and dropping into the valley below Mount Stone before climbing the ridge west of Stone toward Hopper.
row.turnaround: Given the roughly 14-mile one-way approach and an off-trail final scramble with sparse cairns, set a firm turnaround time on summit day that leaves ample margin to get back through the off-trail section and onto the maintained trail before dark, accounting for possible stream-crossing delays.
row.comms: No reliable cell coverage along the North Fork Skokomish River Trail or on the summit — this is deep wilderness terrain. A satellite communicator or PLB is strongly recommended given the remoteness and the multi-day nature of most trips.
row.descent: Reverse the route, descending open slopes and any snow back toward the First Divide / Marmot Lake.

row.detailed_rack: No technical rack is used on the standard class 2 route — it is unroped scrambling on talus, heather, and a short rocky ridge. Some parties carry an ice axe (and occasionally microspikes) for lingering snow patches on north aspects in June/early July.
pro_tips: Reserve your Olympic NP wilderness permit on recreation.gov as early as possible — summer reservations release mid-April and the Skokomish/Duckabush zones fill quickly.

The Home Sweet Home Trail over First Divide is closed along with the Staircase side, so the Duckabush route via Marmot Lake is not an open alternative either; once it reopens, budget roughly double the approach mileage and extra days.
watch_out: The North Fork Skokomish/Staircase approach trail and the Home Sweet Home Trail over First Divide have been closed since the 2025 Bear Gulch Fire, with no reopening date on the park's trail-conditions page updated September 14, 2026 — check the park's trail status before planning either side.
Above Home Sweet Home/First Divide the route is unmarked and off-trail; carry a map/compass or a GPS track.
row.pro_needs: No technical pro; an ice axe is useful for early-season snow on the approach slopes.
row.best_season: Late June through early October is the general climbing window, but the most reliably snow-free travel is mid-July through September; First Divide (4,688 ft) and the upper mountain commonly hold snow into July, requiring an ice axe and possibly traction.
row.approach: The historic Staircase (North Fork Skokomish) approach has been closed since the 2025 Bear Gulch Fire, and the Duckabush approach described here is cut too: the Home Sweet Home Trail from the Duckabush River Trail junction over First Divide is also closed, with no reopening date on the park's trail-conditions page (updated September 14, 2026), so no open trail reaches First Divide while the closure stands. The Duckabush approach starts at the Duckabush Trailhead via Duckabush Trail #803. The tread starts easy for about 2.4 miles to Little Hump, then climbs the steep, loose-rock switchbacks of Big Hump before mellowing again to the Olympic National Park boundary around mile 6.2-6.7. Continue up the valley past 5 Mile Camp (a popular fishing/camping flat by the river) and 10 Mile Camp (~mile 12), where the trail's grade eases through old-growth forest along the Duckabush River — reliable water the whole way, though treat it. Beyond 10 Mile Camp the trail steepens again through the rougher upper-valley tread toward the Duckabush Camp junction with the O'Neil Pass/North Fork Skokomish Trail; from there it's a tough, sustained climb — the last mile notably steep — up to Marmot Lake (roughly 20-21 miles from the trailhead), a good base camp near Hart Lake (0.9 mi), Lake LaCrosse (1.4 mi), and O'Neil Pass (1.2 mi). From Marmot Lake, drop back to the Home Sweet Home junction and climb the Home Sweet Home Trail over First Divide (4,688 ft) — closed along with the Staircase side while the Bear Gulch Fire closure stands — then leave maintained trail to angle cross-country/climber's-path up open talus and subalpine meadow toward Mount Hopper's basin below the summit rockwall (high point ~6,120 ft). This upper stretch has real route-finding difficulty: numerous gullies and ribs look equally plausible from below, snow can choke the gully well into summer (ice axe advisable), and the final scramble features loose rock underfoot — expect to backtrack if you pick the wrong line. Given the mileage (~29 miles one-way), most parties treat this as a multi-day trip with a camp at Marmot Lake (or, once its trail reopens, Home Sweet Home) rather than a car-to-car push.
row.descent_text: Descend by reversing the ascent line: downclimb the same gully/rib system off the summit rockwall back down through the steepest rock step, then the easier talus and heather below it, back to the basin and First Divide (4,688 ft). This is a scramble route with no fixed anchors or bolted stations reported anywhere on it — the standard descent is careful downclimbing, facing in through the steeper rocky steps near the top where the wall lays back into a short climbable face. Some parties uncomfortable reversing that headwall step opt for a single, short rappel off a natural anchor (slung horn or block — bring webbing/cord, since none is fixed in place) to protect the crux; this is optional, not required, so plan on 0 fixed rappels for a typical descent. Watch for loose rock and rockfall onto any party below in the gully system, and re-identify your ascent gully carefully from above — the same routefinding hazard (many similar-looking gullies and ribs) applies in reverse and is arguably worse on the way down. From First Divide, drop back through Home Sweet Home meadow and follow the connector trail down to Marmot Lake, then reverse the Duckabush Trail #803 all the way to the Duckabush Trailhead (an easier but long walk-out, ~29 miles from the high basin). If the historic Staircase approach reopens in the future, the equivalent reversal would instead drop from First Divide down the North Fork Skokomish Trail to Staircase.
row.bail: Retreat by reversing the route; there is no quick exit from this interior peak.

June.reason: Full snow conditions typically persist on the approach and summit through this period; steep snow travel skills required and route-finding is harder under snow cover

August.reason: Matches the best window — snow has generally receded to meadow/talus travel, most stable conditions of the season

October.reason: Outside the season window; this is a short, storm-prone shoulder season for the area

September.reason: Still within the best-season; stable late-summer conditions but shorter days and rising chance of early storms

weather.typical: Cool maritime interior climate; weather can change quickly far from any trailhead, and this route's long approach means limited fast-bailout options if conditions turn.
weather.probability: Afternoon cloud buildups/thunderstorms are possible July-August; storm risk rises into September.

seasonal_hazards.exposure: Moderate slip/fall exposure — loose talus and meadow slopes plus steep snow (early season) on the upper mountain. Class 2 scrambling itself is not highly exposed, but a slip on steep snow or loose talus this far from help is a serious consequence; the dominant risk factor is the very long, remote approach rather than technical terrain.

seasonal_hazards.crevasses: N/A - no glacier travel; the route crosses talus, meadow, and seasonal snow slopes rather than glaciated terrain

approach_variants.name: First Divide from the Duckabush and Marmot Lake
approach_variants.notes: The historic Skokomish approach is closed by fire damage, and so is this one where it leaves the Duckabush: the park lists the Home Sweet Home Trail, from the Duckabush River Trail junction over First Divide, closed for the 2025 Bear Gulch Fire with no reopening date (trail-conditions page updated September 14, 2026), so no open trail reaches First Divide while the closure stands. When it reopens, the way in is the long Duckabush valley over Big Hump to Marmot Lake, then back to the Home Sweet Home junction and over First Divide. Roughly double the old distance and firmly a multi-day trip with a camp at the lake or at Home Sweet Home.
hazards: Loose talus and steep meadow slopes on the upper mountain
Snow choking the summit gully well into summer
Rockfall in the gully system onto anyone below
Burn-scar hazard trees and rockfall along the closed Skokomish corridor
A very long, remote walk-out from anywhere on the route
approach_variants.baseFinding: First Divide is a distinct saddle with Duckabush and Steel to the west and Hopper to the east, and the old climbers' way to the peak splits off here. Do not expect to find it — that tread has been under brush for more than a decade, so treat the saddle itself as the base of the off-trail travel and navigate rather than follow. From the divide, angle east through forest and brush and pop out into open summit meadow, then climb talus toward the rockwall below the top. The identification that actually matters is up there, not at the saddle: several gullies and ribs seam that wall and every one of them looks plausible from the bottom. The one that goes is the line that keeps laying back into short climbable steps; anything that walls up into a blank corner above you is the wrong one, and the honest expectation is that you may back off one and try another. Note a feature at the foot of whichever gully you commit to, because picking it out again from above is harder than finding it from below. The final crest narrows and is impassable in places, so choose your line early.

bivy.name: Home Sweet Home — the meadow camp under First Divide for Steel and Hopper
bivy.notes: THE base camp for the First Divide peaks, sitting in big open meadow about half a mile beyond the divide and roughly 400 ft below it, some 13 to 13.5 miles and 3,800 ft from Staircase. Mount Steel stands about a mile west-northwest of the divide and Mount Hopper about a mile east, so from here both are scrambles rather than expeditions — the two together are commonly done as one long trip of around 32 miles and 4,400 ft total. Hopper can also be taken straight up the slope west from camp instead of using the way trail lower down. This is also the hinge for Mount Duckabush: from the meadow the trail drops north to the Upper Duckabush junction, and the peaks at the head of that valley open up from there. The mileage is the whole story with this camp. It is a two-day walk in for most parties carrying gear, which is why the peaks above it see so little traffic, and why splitting the approach at Camp Pleasant or Nine Stream is the normal way to do it. Wildflowers through July and August, stargazing, and open ground that catches weather — it is exposed, and there is no shelter on the divide itself. Season is roughly mid-July through September; snow holds on the divide and on the north-facing slopes of Steel well into summer.
bivy.water: Reliable through the summer from the headwater creek draining the meadow toward the Duckabush, though the flow drops noticeably by September; fill low rather than at the divide, which has none
bivy.permit: A wilderness permit is required. This is not one of the named quota camps, so it is far easier to get than Flapjack Lakes, but it still has to be reserved through the federal recreation booking site and it does see demand on fine summer weekends. Bear canisters are required — black bears work this meadow regularly. CAMPFIRES ARE PROHIBITED, well above the 3,500 ft line. Stock is permitted on the valley trail, so expect to share the camp occasionally.
bivy.capacity: A small number of sites spread through open subalpine meadow with a privy; it does not hold large numbers well and the meadow is fragile, so stay on the established pads

bivy.name: Upper Duckabush junction camp — the link between First Divide and the Duckabush head
bivy.notes: This is a connector rather than a destination, and it matters because of where it sits: the point where the trail down from First Divide and Home Sweet Home meets the Duckabush River trail coming up from the east and the O'Neil Pass trail heading west. If you are going for Mount Duckabush from Staircase, you come over First Divide, drop to this junction, and climb again toward Marmot Lake or O'Neil Pass — so the day involves losing about 1,600 ft off the divide and regaining it, which is the reason the peak feels harder than its distance suggests. Camping here is what makes that carry manageable. It is deep valley forest with no views, and it is a long way from anywhere in every direction; treat it as a place to sleep between two big days rather than a base for anything.
bivy.water: Reliable — the Duckabush River at the junction
bivy.permit: A wilderness permit is required, reserved through the federal recreation booking site; not a quota camp and usually available. Bear canisters are required. Below the fire line, so fires are allowed in the established rings outside seasonal bans.
bivy.capacity: A modest forested camp at the trail junction, a few sites; lightly used because almost everyone is passing through

row.name: Standard Route (Ares Tower)
row.fa: Fred Beckey and Herb Staley, May 31, 1952 (first ascent of Ares Tower, the ridge's high point)
gear: Light rack (a few small cams/stoppers) and a rope for the short low-5th-class step near the summit
Helmet — loose rock on the approach talus and along the ridge
Extra sling/cord to inspect and, if needed, back up the summit rappel anchor (not agency-maintained)
Trekking poles and gaiters for loose talus and any lingering early-season snow on the approach
hazards: Loose, scree-covered talus on the initial descent from the roadside pullout to Early Winters Creek
Early-season crossing of Early Winters Creek on logs can be swift and high with snowmelt
Rockfall on the ridge, especially with other parties above or in unsettled weather
Afternoon thunderstorms are common on the exposed ridge crest in summer
Route-finding: Vasiliki Tower, The Acropolis, and Niki Tower are similar granite towers on the same ridge crest and are easy to mistake for Ares Tower, the true high point
row.overview: Ares Tower is the highest of several named granite spires — Charon Tower, The Acropolis, Ares Tower, Vasiliki Tower, the Juno-Jupiter Towers, Aphrodite Tower, and Baccus Tower — strung along Vasiliki Ridge, which radiates north from the Wine Spires/Silver Star Mountain massif above Washington Pass. Fred Beckey and Herb Staley made the first ascent of the ridge on May 31, 1952; Beckey named it after Vasiliki Dwyer, a woman he met at Stevens Pass — the only Cascades feature he ever named after a woman. Despite its imposing look from the highway, Ares Tower itself is a moderate objective: essentially a 4th-class scramble to a notch just north of the true summit, finished by a short low-5th-class step (or an alternate direct low-5th variation up the west face).
row.beta: This is the standard line up the ridge's true high point, first climbed by Fred Beckey and Herb Staley in 1952. From Burgundy Col, work north along/just below the ridge crest on 4th-class rock to a notch on the north side of the summit block, then scramble south around the west side of a large summit boulder to the base of a short low-5th-class step that gains the true summit. An old fixed rappel anchor sits at the top for the descent. Most parties do it as a long day from the Washington Pass pullout, and many combine it with the neighboring Acropolis and Niki Tower to the south for an efficient multi-summit day on the ridge.
row.turnaround: Set a firm turnaround; the rock pitches and rappels take time
row.rock_grade: low-mid 5th class (4th class terrain plus one short low-5th-class/~5.4 step to the true summit)
row.rappels: 1 rappel from an old fixed anchor near the summit to retreat down the short low-5th-class step; the remainder of the route downclimbs on 4th-class terrain.
row.permit: No climbing or wilderness permit required; Northwest Forest Pass (or day fee) to park at developed trailheads.
row.comms: No cell service through the Washington Pass corridor / North Cascades Highway backcountry — this is a well-documented dead zone with no services of any kind at the pass. Carry a satellite communicator or PLB; do not rely on a phone signal for a call-out.
row.descent: Descend via the standard descent route, retracing the ascent when possible. Be aware of loose rock and snow bridge hazards. Maintain group cohesion on exposed sections.

row.detailed_rack: Standard alpine rock rack (cams and nuts) with slings for the spire pitches
pro_tips: Camp at 'the Bench' (~6,460 ft) or Burgundy Col to shorten the summit day, and combine Ares Tower with the nearby Acropolis and Niki Tower for a bigger ridge day, as most parties do
The unsigned 'Wine Spires' pullout used for this approach does not require a Northwest Forest Pass, unlike the paved Blue Lake Trailhead a short drive away
Early Winters Campground (fee, first-come first-served) is a convenient car-camp base the night before starting the approach
watch_out: Confirm you're on Ares Tower itself before committing to the technical step — several similar towers (Vasiliki Tower, The Acropolis, Niki Tower) sit along the same ridge
Visually inspect the summit rappel anchor before weighting it; it's a climber-placed/replaced anchor with no official maintenance
Snow can linger on the north-facing approach benches (~6,200 ft) well into late June or July in a heavy winter
row.pro_needs: Rock protection on the technical pitches; belayed climbing
row.best_season: Late June through September is the practical window. The route isn't accessible at all until SR-20 (North Cascades Highway) reopens for the season and the Early Winters Creek approach trail melts out — snow can linger on the north-facing benches around 6,200 ft well into late June or July in a heavy winter (in 2026, storm-damage repairs delayed the highway's full reopening to June 14). Afternoon thunderstorms become more frequent by August; stable, cool weather often extends the season into September.
row.approach: Park at the unsigned 'Wine Spires' pullout on SR-20, about 3.7 miles east of Washington Pass (roughly 0.7 mile past the Cutthroat Lake Road turnoff, near milepost 166), at about 4,300 ft elevation. A boot path drops down loose, scree-covered talus into the trees, passes a trail register, and crosses Early Winters Creek on logs at about 4,080 ft. The trail then climbs steadily through forest, steepening between two side creeks, gaining roughly 3,700+ ft to Burgundy Col (~7,800 ft); a flat bench campsite ('the Bench,' ~6,460 ft) sits about halfway up and is the more common camp for this objective. Vasiliki Ridge and Ares Tower rise directly north of Burgundy Col and the Wine Spires camp area; from the bench or col, contour and scramble north along the ridge crest to reach the base of Ares Tower.
row.descent_text: Rappel from the fixed anchor at the Ares Tower summit down to the notch to retrieve stashed gear, then reverse the 4th-class ridge scramble and descend the Burgundy Col approach trail back to Early Winters Creek and the SR-20 pullout.
row.bail: Rappel from the highest reached anchor

pitch_detail.notes: From Burgundy Col, work north along/just below the ridge crest on 4th-class granite to the notch just north of the true summit.
Short, exposed roped move out of the notch (scramble around the west side of a large summit boulder) to gain the true summit; old fixed rap anchor at the top.

itinerary.cal: Only feasible once North Cascades Highway 20 opens over Washington Pass for the season (typically mid-April until a winter closure between mid-November and early December, weather dependent).

days.note: From the Wine Spires pullout on Hwy 20 (~3.7 mi east of Washington Pass), drop steeply down to and cross Early Winters Creek, then climb the well-used climber's trail through timber and talus to the Bench, an established camp at ~6,460 ft with a nearby spring. Stronger parties push on another ~1,300 ft to camp at Burgundy Col itself (~7,800 ft) to shorten summit day.

access.fees: None at the roadside pullout. If car-camping the night before, Early Winters Campground (first-come, first-served, open roughly April-November) charges a nightly fee.
access.notes: Not inside North Cascades National Park — this corridor is entirely Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest (Methow Valley Ranger District). No Mount Rainier-style climbing fee applies here.
access.rules: No climbing or wilderness permit required for day climbing. Dispersed camping capped at 10 days; no camping within ¼ mile of Cutthroat Lake; no campfires at dispersed sites; bear-resistant food storage required; dogs on leash ≤6 ft.
access.permit: No climbing or wilderness permit is required; the Forest Service's regional climbing/caving page lists no permit requirement for the Silver Star/Wine Spires/Vasiliki Ridge area.
access.closures: SR-20 (North Cascades Highway) is gated and closed to all traffic every winter, typically reopening mid-to-late April, but reopening can slip well into June after a heavy snow year or storm damage — in 2026, washouts and a slope failure near Diablo Lake delayed full reopening until June 14. The approach trail itself is a further limiting factor: it often isn't snow-free until several weeks after the highway opens.
access.seasonal: WA-20 (North Cascades Highway) closes gate-to-gate from roughly mid-November or early December until mid/late April; the entire Washington Pass corridor is car-inaccessible in winter.
access.landManager: Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, Methow Valley Ranger District (Winthrop, WA); Forest Supervisor's Office in Wenatchee, (509) 664-9200
access.land_manager: Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest (Methow Valley Ranger District)
access.parking_pass: Northwest Forest Pass required at Washington Pass Overlook, Blue Lake, and Cutthroat trailheads — $5/day or $30/annual (America the Beautiful pass also honored).
access.passRequired: None at the unsigned 'Wine Spires' pullout used for this approach. This differs from the nearby, developed Blue Lake Trailhead (a short drive further east/west), which does require a Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass.

overnight_permit.where: Nothing to obtain for a night on the climbers' trails. The Early Winters valley campgrounds charge a nightly fee.

climate.fall: Cool, often stable weather in September into October, before the highway closes for the season
climate.spring: Snowpack lingers on the approach trail and gully into June
climate.summer: Warm, mostly dry days with a real risk of building afternoon thunderstorms
climate.winter: Highway closed; deep snowpack and high avalanche hazard make the approach a winter travel/ski objective, not a climbing one
climate.typical: Dry, sunny North Cascades alpine summer weather is the norm on this east-of-the-crest ridge, but conditions can turn quickly; afternoon thunderstorms and sudden temperature drops are common on the exposed ridge crest.

bySeason.fall: Often stable and cool through September and into early October, but nights are cold and an early-season storm can dust the ridge with snow with little warning.
bySeason.spring: Approach trail and ridge typically still snow-covered into June; expect postholing and lingering snow patches on the north-facing benches.
bySeason.summer: Prime climbing window (late June-August); snow can still linger around 6,200 ft into early July in heavy-snow years. Watch for building afternoon cumulus and thunderstorms.
bySeason.winter: SR-20 is closed by snow gates; the approach is not accessible.

emergency.notes: Cell coverage at Washington Pass and on this approach is unreliable to nonexistent. A May 2025 rappel-anchor-failure accident in the nearby Liberty Bell Group (same access corridor) required the sole survivor to hike out and drive roughly 40 miles before he found a working pay phone in Newhalem to call for help — even that town had no reliable cell service, underscoring how remote self-rescue and communication are in this stretch of SR-20.
emergency.rangerStation: Methow Valley Ranger District, Winthrop, WA (Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest)
emergency.nearestHospital: No hospital in the Methow Valley itself; the nearest full-service hospitals are Three Rivers Hospital in Brewster, WA and Mid-Valley Hospital in Omak, WA, both roughly 60+ miles from Washington Pass via SR-20/US-97.
emergency.sheriffDispatch: Okanogan County Sheriff's Office via 911; mountain rescues in this area are coordinated by Okanogan County Search & Rescue (OCSAR) alongside the U.S. Forest Service and, at times, the Winthrop Marshal's Office.

approach_variants.name: The Wine Spires pullout to the Bench, then NORTH along the ridge crest to Ares Tower
approach_variants.notes:
Park at the unsigned Wine Spires pullout on SR-20, about 3.7 miles east of Washington Pass, roughly 0.7 mile past the Cutthroat Lake Road turnoff near milepost 166, at about 4,300 ft. A boot path drops down loose scree-covered talus into the trees, passes a trail register, and crosses Early Winters Creek on logs at about 4,080 ft.

The trail then climbs steadily through forest, steepening between two side creeks, gaining roughly 3,700-plus ft to Burgundy Col at about 7,800 ft. A flat bench campsite, the Bench, at about 6,460 ft sits about halfway up AND IS THE MORE COMMON CAMP FOR THIS OBJECTIVE than the col itself.
hazards: A class 4 ridge traverse with real exposure to reach the tower
Loose scree-covered talus on the initial drop from the highway
A log crossing of Early Winters Creek
The whole approach shares a trail with the Wine Spires objectives and then deliberately departs from it
approach_variants.baseFinding:
VASILIKI RIDGE AND ARES TOWER RISE DIRECTLY NORTH OF BURGUNDY COL AND THE WINE SPIRES CAMP AREA. SO THE TEST IS DIRECTIONAL AND IT IS THE OPPOSITE OF EVERY OTHER ROUTE FROM THIS TRAILHEAD: FROM THE BENCH OR THE COL, GO NORTH.

Every Wine Spires objective, Burgundy, Chianti, Pernod, Chablis, is reached by going to Burgundy Col and then SOUTH or EAST from it. Ares Tower is the one you reach by contouring and scrambling NORTH along the ridge crest. IF YOU HAVE DROPPED ONTO SNOW BENEATH AN EAST-FACING WALL, YOU HAVE GONE SOUTH AND YOU ARE UNDER THE WINE SPIRES.

ARRIVAL: Ares Tower is the HIGH POINT of Vasiliki Ridge at about 8,190 ft. Following the crest north, you are at the base when the ridge stops being scrambleable and rises into a tower. The climbing is a 4th-class scramble to a notch, then one short low-5th-class step to the true summit; Grade II-III.

CONFIRM BY THE HARDWARE, AND ON THIS ridge IT IS THE ONE PIECE OF FIXED GEAR WORTH KNOWING ABOUT: THERE IS A FIXED ANCHOR AT THE ARES TOWER SUMMIT, and the standard descent is a single rappel from it down to the notch to retrieve stashed gear, then a reversal of the fourth-class ridge scramble.

SO THE PATTERN OF THE DAY IS: stash gear at a notch below the tower, climb the short summit step, rappel back to your gear. If there is nowhere sensible to leave a pack, you are not at the tower yet.

CAMP CHOICE AS A PLANNING FACT: the Bench at about 6,460 ft is the more common camp for this objective than Burgundy Col, which is 1,300 ft higher and in the wrong direction.

row.name: Plan 9 from Outer Space
gear: cams to 3 inch (doubles in common sizes)
hazards: Remote, self-rescue-oriented location days from the nearest road, with minimal-to-no cell coverage.
Loose rock on the Barrier crossing and basin-approach traverses.
Exposed simul-climbing required on the summit-ridge descent traverse to the Blob/Terror col.
Seasonal glacier/snowfield moats and crevasses open up on nearby approach terrain as summer progresses into August.
row.overview: A long, moderate alpine rock line up the right-edge buttress of "The Blob," the rock formation just north of the Himmelhorn in the Southern Pickets, finishing across the exposed "Bela Lugosi Traverse" and up a summit dihedral.
row.beta: Plan 9 from Outer Space climbs roughly 16 pitches (~1,400 ft) of varied, mostly moderate rock up the right edge of a prominent buttress on "The Blob." The route crosses the exposed-but-moderate "Bela Lugosi Traverse" below a large ledge, then finishes up a steep dihedral of good rock to the summit. The first-ascent party rated the crux 5.10c; a repeat ascent found an easier line and down-rated it to 5.9, and the route is now given a compromise grade of 5.9+ — as with many alpine routes of this style, the felt difficulty depends heavily on which exact line you choose.
row.turnaround: Given the long, multi-day approach and a remote, self-rescue-only setting far from any road, set a firm turnaround time that leaves ample daylight margin to complete the summit ridge traverse and both rappels, and to be back in camp before afternoon thunderstorms typically build.
row.rappels: 2 rappels from the summit ridge into the Blob–Terror col notch, then downclimb/scramble back to camp
row.face: South Buttress of The Blob (aka The Rake)
row.permit: North Cascades NP complex: no permit for day climbs; all overnight backcountry stays require a backcountry permit (the Terror Basin and Crescent Creek zones are walk-up only, issued in person at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center the day of or the day before the trip).
row.comms: Cell coverage in the Southern Pickets is minimal to absent. NPS guidance for North Cascades climbers notes that cell calls from park backcountry, when they connect at all, often route to dispatch centers far from the actual location, delaying response — a satellite communicator is strongly advised rather than relying on phone service.
row.descent: Traverse the Blob's summit ridge north to the Blob/Terror col, then make 2 rappels from webbing anchors into the notch below.
obj_haz: loose rock (choss) off the described line, typical of Skagit Gneiss in the Pickets
exposed, unprotected Class 3 terrain crossing 'The Barrier' on approach
remote multi-day approach with no quick rescue access
no fixed anchors anywhere on route or descent (aside from old webbing at the col)
weather can close in fast on the long, exposed summit ridge

timing.recommendedStart: Pre-dawn/alpine start from the Crescent Creek Basin camp to allow a full day for the 16-pitch route plus the summit-ridge traverse and col rappels back to camp.

row.detailed_rack: A standard alpine rock rack up to 3 inches — a single set of cams with doubles in the common finger-to-hand sizes given the route's length — plus a set of stoppers and extra slings for the exposed traverses. There are no fixed anchors on the route itself; the only fixed gear (webbing rap anchors) is on the descent at the Blob/Terror col.
what_to_bring: sturdy approach shoes for talus/slab/snow travel
ice axe for early-season snow crossings on the approach
extra water (basins can run dry late season)
map/compass or GPS for the basin and col route-finding
pro_tips: Go in July while snow still eases travel across the Barrier and basin crossings, before August's glacier moats and loose scree complicate the approach.

The route's grade is famously line-dependent — the first-ascent party rated the crux 5.10c, but a repeat party found an easier line and down-graded it to 5.9, so careful route-finding on the buttress changes the difficulty you'll actually encounter.
watch_out: The "Bela Lugosi Traverse" below the summit dihedral is exposed and unnerving even though it's only moderate in technical difficulty.
The descent ridge traverse to the Blob/Terror col is described by the first ascensionists as "an adventure in itself," requiring short simul-climbing over exposed terrain.
The Barrier crossing on approach is loose, dirty class 3 terrain — a slip here would be serious.
row.pro_needs: Gear to 3 inches covers the route; no fixed anchors are encountered while climbing (fixed webbing exists only on the descent rappels).
row.best_season: Late July through September is the usual window. June and early July often still hold more continuous snow that eases travel across the Barrier and basin crossings, but by August Cascade glaciers and snowfields open up with crevasses and moats on nearby approach terrain (noted issues occur around the Otto-Himmel col and Terror Glacier), so timing should be weighed against seasonal melt-out.
row.approach: From the Goodell Creek group-camp trailhead near Newhalem, walk the overgrown Goodell Creek roadbed for about 4 miles to the cairn near the Terror Creek crossing, then climb the Terror Creek climbers' path. The Blob stands above Crescent Creek Basin, so from the Terror Creek side you must cross the Barrier, the loose, brushy ridge dividing the Terror Creek drainage from Crescent Creek; it can be crossed low or high from Terror Basin. Descend into Crescent Creek Basin and camp within reach of the Himmelhorn and the Blob, then scramble to the base of the south buttress. This is a serious multi-day expedition approach requiring a North Cascades National Park backcountry permit, off-trail routefinding through brush and talus, and glacier/snow travel gear.
row.descent_text: From the top, traverse the summit ridge of the Blob northward toward the Blob/Terror col — described by the first-ascent party as "an adventure in itself," with short simul-climbing recommended over the exposed crest. At the col edge, locate webbing rappel anchors over a steep step and make two rappels down into the notch. From the notch, an easy scramble down the col returns climbers to the bench below.
row.bail: Below the Bela Lugosi Traverse, the moderate, varied lower buttress pitches can generally be reversed/rappelled on gear. Above the traverse, it is generally safer to continue to the summit and use the established rappel-and-scramble descent into the Blob/Terror col than to attempt to reverse the exposed traverse itself.
row.itinerary: Typically done as part of a multi-day Southern Pickets trip: Day 1, backpack in via the Goodell Creek roadbed and Terror Creek climbers' path to a high camp near the Barrier or in Terror Basin; Day 2, cross the Barrier into Crescent Creek Basin and establish camp within striking distance of the Himmelhorn/Blob area; Day 3, climb Plan 9 from Outer Space and return to camp via the Blob/Terror col rappels; Day 4, hike out.

July.reason: The south buttress dries while continuous snow still smooths the Barrier crossing and basin travel; the Goodell Creek log crossing runs high early in the month.

June.reason: Terror and Crescent Creek basins are still under deep snow with avalanche runout, and the 16-pitch buttress can hold wet ledges.

August.reason: Rock is at its driest, but moats and crevasses open at the head of the Terror Glacier, making the high Barrier crossing harder.

October.reason: Early autumn snow and ice on the loose Barrier ledges and very short days make the multi-day approach committing.

September.reason: Still climbable via the low Barrier ledges, but bare ice and big moats complicate snow crossings and shorter days squeeze a 16-pitch day.

bivy.name: Terror Basin camp
bivy.notes: The standard base for the south side of the range, and the place the Terror Creek climbers' path is trying to reach. From the flat gravel the basin runs up to a notch on its eastern rim near 6,200 ft, and the Chopping Block, Degenhardt, the Pyramid and the west side of Terror are all workable from here. Whether a party gets this far on day one is genuinely contested — strong parties who know the path do it, and parties who lose the path in the timber routinely do not.
bivy.water: Meltwater off the snowfields above the basin, generally dependable while snow remains and a hunt in a dry late summer. Sources are seasonal, not spring-fed.
bivy.permit: Terror Basin cross-country zone, from Marblemount. 6-person party maximum. It is NOT on the short list of zones reservable in advance, so it is WALK-UP ONLY — up to 24 hours ahead, with permits released in the morning of day one. Fires prohibited; human waste in a cathole, or out in a blue bag above treeline.
bivy.capacity: Small flat gravelly ground for a few tents; the park caps the zone at 6 people per party

bivy.name: Goodell Creek Campground, roadhead staging
bivy.notes: The pavement-level staging camp rather than a mountain camp, and most parties use it to get a few hours of sleep before starting the approach in the dark. Bear boxes, tables and vault toilets mean food and rubbish can be dealt with before you leave the car. Sleeping here advances you toward the peaks not at all, but it does let you hit the roadbed at first light, which matters on an approach this long.
bivy.water: Potable water when the campground is open for the season; the Skagit and Goodell Creek are immediately adjacent as backup
bivy.permit: Frontcountry campground fee only — no wilderness permit needed to sleep here. Reservable through recreation.gov in peak season, first-come outside it; not always open year round, so confirm before counting on it.
bivy.capacity: 19 individual drive-in sites, plus a separate group campground where the old roadbed begins

That is defensible, because the ground above is where the day gets expensive and nobody wants to be finding the path by headlamp. The cost is that the whole climb to the basin still lies ahead, so a low night usually means a full second day of approach with no climbing in it.

Changing only the start would leave the 0.5-hr approach wrong. What would settle it: two reports timing Luna Col to East Fury summit.

earlier_research.correct_value: East Fury ~8,322 ft, the highest point of the traverse
earlier_research.evidence: The 2024 dGPS survey puts East Fury at 8,321.5 ft and an independently compiled topo peak list gives 8,325 ft; both place it above West Fury (~8,300 ft), so the overview's 8,280 ft is wrong and the traverse's high point is East Fury, not West Fury's 8,305.

earlier_research.fact: Overnight permit 'where' says reserve on Recreation.gov for a walk-up-only cross-country zone

earlier_research.evidence: The park's cross-country zone page says only Boston Basin, Eldorado, Sulphide, Price, Triumph and Tapto Lakes can be reserved and all other zones are walk-up only. The Recreation.gov booking system's own quota data for the 'Luna Cross Country Zone II' division shows an online quota of 0 with the walk-up flag set on every date (Boston Basin, by contrast, shows 4 online slots and no walk-up flag), while Luna Camp (a trail camp) is a separate, reservable division. So the high camp zone is walk-up only; only trail camps like Luna Camp can be booked ahead.

earlier_research.fact: Camp the traverse day starts from
earlier_research.correct_value: Traverse day starts at ~6 AM from the Luna Col high camp; Luna Camp is only the first night
earlier_research.evidence: A 2020 party camped at Luna Col, left at 6 AM, climbed East Fury, traversed to West Fury (2.5 h) and returned to Luna Col the same day. A guide service runs day 1 as 9.4 mi to Luna Camp and uses a 7,200 ft Luna high camp as the summit launch point; another party slept night 1 at Luna Camp and nights 2-3 at the Luna-Fury col; a fourth left its Luna Pass camp at 5:30 AM for East Fury. None starts the summit day from Luna Camp in the valley.

earlier_research.correct_value: About 1.5 mi beyond Luna Camp, around 2,460 ft

The USGS DEM at a documented crossing point reads 2,437 ft and at Luna Camp 2,432 ft, so the waypoint's 2,200 ft (below the camp downstream of it) is wrong and 'a short way' understates the distance. The bivy note is not patched (bivy is out of scope) and already says a mile and a half.

The 2.5 h East-to-West traverse figure is corroborated. Would settle it: a second source giving a typical Luna Col to East Fury time so approachTimeHrs and totalHrs can be restated.

row.name: Ridge Traverse from East Fury
gear: Helmet (essential for rockfall and loose rock)
hazards: Chossy, unconsolidated granite prone to failure
Limited solid anchor placements for protection or rappels
Exposure on multiple tower sections with 100+ ft drops
Poor-quality tat on descent - unreliable fixed anchors
Avalanche potential in early season on approaches
row.overview: A wild and exposed scramble traverse connecting East Fury (8,322 ft) to West Fury (8,305 ft), involving three main towers with Class 2-4 descent to saddle and Class 4-5 climbing on towers. This is the standard method of traversing between the two peaks and involves significant exposure, loose rock, and dangerous rappels.
row.beta: Once you have reached the summit of East Fury, you may continue to West Fury via this traverse. The traverse is a series of gendarmes and towers with a combination of scrambling and low 5th class rock. The descent off East Fury to the low saddle is on very loose Class 2-3 boulders. There are three towers you must climb up and over before making the final ascent to the summit of West Fury. A 50-60 meter rope is recommended at the very least for rappelling the 4th and low 5th class areas you have climbed.
row.turnaround: Turnaround at 2:00 PM from West Fury summit to ensure sufficient daylight for descent. If significant snow is encountered on the approach glacier, reassess the route. Party consensus and comfort level with loose rock should determine go/no-go decision before committing to first tower.
row.rappels: About 6 rappels, reversing the towers you climbed. Station lengths are not established - this route carries a single 50-60 m rope, which doubled reaches only 25-30 m. Anchors are poor-quality placements on chossy rock and unreliable fixed tat, and each rappel makes retreat progressively more difficult.
row.face: Connecting ridge crest between the East Fury and West Fury summits
row.permit: North Cascades NP complex: no permit for day climbs; all overnight backcountry stays require a backcountry permit (reserve on Recreation.gov or walk-up at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center).
row.comms: No cellular service available on the peak. Satellite communication device (e.g., Garmin InReach, SPOT) recommended for emergency communication in this remote area. Verizon occasionally has coverage at Ross Lake trailhead (about 2,100 ft).
row.descent: Traverse back to East Fury summit via the same route (downclimbing towers and using rappels), then descend East Fury via the Southeast Glacier and Class 3 terrain back to Luna Camp and Luna Col, then descend the Access Creek basin to the Big Beaver Trail.
obj_haz: Extremely loose, chossy rock and mobile talus on both summit blocks
Residual snow/ice on the towers into mid-summer
Minimal reliable protection - solid gear placements are scarce

waypoints.name: Ross Dam Trailhead (SR-20) — via Ross Lake water taxi/hike to Big Beaver, then off-trail to Access Creek/Luna Camp
waypoints.note: Road-accessible trailhead on SR-20 (MP 134-135) at Ross Dam/Ross Lake Resort. Parties either walk ~6 mi along the west shore of Ross Lake or take the Ross Lake Resort water taxi to the Big Beaver Trail junction, hike ~9.4 mi up Big Beaver Trail to Luna Camp, then go off-trail up Access Creek to the Luna-Fury col before climbing East Fury and traversing the connecting ridge (three towers) to reach West Fury.
waypoints.directions: Drive SR-20, the North Cascades Highway, to the Ross Dam Trailhead near milepost 134-135; this is the last road access of the trip and the car stays here for the duration. From the parking it is a 15-20 minute descent to Ross Lake. Most parties then arrange a paid water taxi from Ross Lake Resort to the Big Beaver Trail landing rather than walking the roughly 6 miles of west-shore lakeshore trail, and the same taxi is how you get back out.

waypoints.name: Access Creek Junction
waypoints.note: Leave Big Beaver Trail to ascend Access Creek toward the Southern Pickets.

waypoints.name: Access Col
waypoints.note: Gains the crest between Access Creek and Luna Cirque.

waypoints.name: Luna Col
waypoints.note: High col below Luna Peak; standard approach to the Fury massif.

waypoints.name: Loose Tower Traverse
waypoints.note: Descend to a low saddle then climb over three loose towers, low 5th class; rope recommended for rappels.

row.detailed_rack: A modest rock climbing rack is essential due to poor anchor placements throughout. Bring 1-2 sets of small cams (0.4-1.5 inches) and a set of nuts for protection and rappel anchors. Many parties report difficulty finding solid rock for gear placement; natural features (trees, rocks) may be used for anchors where possible.
what_to_bring: Water and high-calorie food for summit day
Sat communication device (Garmin InReach or SPOT)
pro_tips: This traverse is almost always soloed due to the difficulty of protecting on chossy rock
Bring extra cordage for redundant rappel anchors
Scout the descent route carefully before committing; retreat becomes progressively difficult
Expect the traverse to take about two and a half hours each way, and allow a full day for the round trip if rope work is needed
Excellent scrambling skills and comfort with exposure are essential
watch_out: Extremely loose and chossy granite throughout - rockfall hazard
Very difficult to place protection or establish secure rappel anchors
Three exposed towers with substantial drop-offs - exposure and fall hazard
Poor-quality rock can crumble when weighted - test handholds carefully
High altitude (8,300 ft) and remote location - limited escape options
Retreat becomes increasingly difficult once you begin rappelling
row.pro_needs: Protection is difficult to place due to chossy, loose granite. Many climbing parties find it nearly impossible to establish solid anchor points and often rely on natural features or accept marginal protection. Rappels are typically established using multiple strands and directional placements to increase security.
row.best_season: Mid-July to late August presents the most stable conditions with minimal remaining snow. Early season (May-June) may have significant snow covering terrain and requiring different techniques. September is possible in stable weather years, but approaching winter storms are a concern.
row.approach: Drive SR-20 (North Cascades Highway) to the Ross Dam Trailhead and walk down to Ross Lake, where most parties take the paid water taxi from Ross Lake Resort to the Big Beaver landing rather than walking the lakeshore trail. From the landing it is about 9.4 miles of nearly flat old-growth trail up the Big Beaver valley to Luna Camp, the usual first night. About a mile and a half beyond camp, leave the trail on a small boot path and cross Big Beaver Creek just north of where Access Creek comes in, around 2,460 ft. Depending on the year this is a log or a wade. Then climb the north side of Access Creek on a faint, brushy climbers' path through Access Creek basin, up the south gully and around the south side of Luna Peak to Luna Col, the usual high camp. From Luna Col, follow the ridge toward Fury over class 3 ground with many short ups and downs. Drop to traverse heather slopes on its south side to the Southeast Glacier near 6,700 ft, then climb the right side of the glacier to steeper snow and a possible bergschrund below East Fury's summit, where the traverse to the West Peak begins. Allow three to five days for the round trip. In summer 2026 wildfire closed the Big Beaver Trail from Big Beaver Stock Camp to Stillwell Camp, including Luna Camp, with no cross-country travel from closed trails, so check current closures with North Cascades National Park before planning.
row.descent_text: Descend the towers you climbed by reversing the route and setting rappels off poor-quality anchors on chossy rock. Each rappel down makes retreat progressively more difficult. Once off the traverse, descend the east side of East Fury to the saddle on loose Class 2-3 talus, then descend the Southeast Glacier back to Luna Col and the main Access Creek drainage.
row.bail: If conditions deteriorate or party is uncomfortable, downclimb the first tower and descend east side of East Fury. Early retreat to the tower areas is still possible, but continued rappelling becomes increasingly committing. There are no bailout routes once committed to the middle towers.

pitch_detail.notes: Loose talus down to the East Fury-West Fury saddle
Bypassed via ~100 ft descent on steep snow to a class 4 rock ramp, then heather/slabs to the notch between towers 1 and 2
South-bending scree ramp around the north side; a narrow ledge behind the tower leads to more steep scree
Several low-5th moves via a notch approached from the north, then exposed slabs
Four more gendarmes; downclimb or rappel around/right of the first, then weave up, over, and around the rest
Traverse sideways from the last notch over sloping slabs, past several more pinnacles, to the true West Fury summit

row.itinerary: Day 1: Water taxi from Ross Dam to Big Beaver, hike 9.4 miles to Luna Camp. Day 2: Climb Access Creek and Access Col to a high camp at Luna Col. Day 3: From Luna Col, ascend East Fury, traverse to West Fury, and return over East Fury to Luna Col. Day 4: Descend Access Creek and the Big Beaver Trail to Ross Lake for the water taxi return.

access.fees: Backcountry permit: $10 per person aged 16 and over, plus a $6 non-refundable reservation fee. The park has no entrance fee.
access.notes: 60% of sites are reservable in advance via Recreation.gov; the remaining 40% are walk-up, obtained in person the day before at the Wilderness Information Center in Marblemount.
access.rules: Group size capped at 6 in off-trail cross-country zones (which includes most Picket Range approaches; 12 in on-trail corridors). Bear canisters required in some zones — free loaners at permit offices.
access.closures: Luna Fire closure (as of mid-September 2026): the Big Beaver Trail is closed from Big Beaver Stock Camp to Stillwell Camp, and Luna Camp, Beaver Pass Camp (with its stock and group camps) and 39 Mile Camp (with 39 Mile Stock) are closed; cross-country zone access from closed trails is prohibited. The closure moves - check current park fire closures before a trip.

access.land_manager: National Park Service — North Cascades National Park (Stephen Mather Wilderness)

overnight_permit.what: North Cascades NP backcountry permit (cross-country zone), fee per person, not free
overnight_permit.where: The Luna cross-country zone cannot be reserved; get a walk-up permit in person at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center. Hannegan-side permits can also be picked up at the Glacier Public Service Center on its limited summer days.

road.name: Ross Lake Trailhead (Highway 20) + Ross Lake Resort water taxi to Big Beaver Trailhead
road.status: Highway 20 is fully paved to the Ross Lake trailhead pullout; the trailhead sits at the western end of the seasonal winter closure (milepost 134), and later in winter the closure point is usually moved down to Newhalem (milepost 120), which cuts off road access to the trailhead. Most parties use the Ross Lake Resort water taxi (fee, reservation required) to avoid roughly 6 miles of lakeshore hiking to reach the Big Beaver Trailhead, since there is no direct road/trail shortcut.
road.driveNote: Trailhead is about 13.4 miles east of Newhalem on Highway 20 — roughly 2.5-3 hours from Seattle. This is a multi-day expedition approach beyond the trailhead (9+ miles of maintained trail to Luna Camp, then off-trail travel).
road.seasonalGate: The Ross Lake Resort water taxi operates seasonally (roughly summer only); outside that season parties must hike the lakeshore trail instead.

climate.fall: September: Earlier storms bring significant precipitation. Temperatures dropping rapidly. October approaches winter conditions.
climate.spring: May-June: Rapid snowmelt creates hazardous avalanche conditions and stream crossings. Temperatures still below freezing above 7,000 ft at night.
climate.summer: Jul-Aug: Most stable conditions with 40-50F daytime highs at altitude, occasional clear days between weather systems. Wet and heavy snow if it falls.
climate.winter: Nov-Apr: Extreme avalanche danger, frequent white-out conditions, deep snow. Access restricted by road closure. Only winter mountaineers with specialized skills should attempt.
climate.typical: Cold and wet with frequent storms. Marine influence from Pacific Ocean brings persistent moisture, especially west-facing slopes. Wind can be severe at altitude.

emergency.notes: Rescue from West Peak is extremely difficult and may take 12+ hours due to remote location. Evacuation by helicopter is weather-dependent and often impossible. Self-rescue mindset essential. Sat phone/InReach strongly recommended.
